item.title: The Night Count
item.description: At two in the morning, a pharmacist finds a blister pack holding more tablets than the register allows, and the number keeps climbing. Someone has been checking his work every night for years, and he has never looked at the second signature.
item.content:encoded:
At two in the morning, Beaumont Row Pharmacy hummed. The fridge for the insulin hummed, and so did the strip light over the dispensing bench. Frank Farnsworth had stopped hearing either of them years ago.

He took the key from his lanyard and opened the controlled-drugs cupboard. It was steel, bolted to the wall, with a door that always stuck at the last inch. He put his hip against it, as he did every night, and it gave.

The register lay open on the bench. He ran his pencil down the page. Diazepam, correct. Oxycodone, correct. Methadone, correct. He counted each box aloud, softly, because the habit kept him honest. His own voice was company at that hour.

Then he reached the bottom shelf. A single blister pack sat behind the tramadol, a flat white card with a pharmacy label on it. Morphine sulphate, ten milligram tablets. The register said nine remaining.

He tipped the pack under the light and counted the cells. Eleven tablets.

"No," he said.

He counted again, touching each cell with the end of his pencil. Eleven. Two more than the book. Two more than he had any right to hold.

Frank sat down on the stool. Shortages happened. Everyone knew the cure for a shortage, and it was paperwork and a phone call to the superintendent. Nobody had a cure for a surplus. Surplus meant that something had come in, and nothing had come in.

He read the label. The print was the old type, from the printer they'd thrown out when the new system arrived. Patient: Mallory, Victor. Dispensed by: F. Farnsworth. The date was six years ago this month.

He remembered nothing about the man. That bothered him more than it should have done. He remembered most scripts. He remembered the regulars and the odd ones, and the woman who always paid in coins. But Mallory, Victor was only a name on a card.

He went to the back office and found the old collection ledger. It was a ring binder with a green spine. He turned to the right month and found the line. Mallory. Morphine sulphate 10 mg. Not collected. Stock returned to cupboard. His own initials sat beside it.

So the pack had been there six years. Nine tablets, written off and forgotten. He had checked this cupboard on hundreds of nights and never once questioned the card behind the tramadol.

"Nine," he said, back at the bench. "It was nine."

He counted a third time, slowly, saying each number aloud. At eleven his voice stopped.

Then he did what the regulations required. He wrote the figure he could prove. He signed the register, Farnsworth, 2.07 a.m., and beside the line he wrote nine, because nine was the number that closed the book. Then, in smaller writing, he added eleven in brackets, and did not like the look of it.

He lifted the pack to slide it back onto the shelf. That was when he saw the foil.

One cell near the corner was empty. Its foil was sealed flat and silver, the way it should be. Only now it wasn't flat. It stood up very slightly in the middle, a faint blister of metal, as if something beneath it was pressing out.

Frank held the pack still. The fridge hummed. The foil did not move again.

He put his thumb beside it, not on it, and found he was waiting to feel it breathe.

• • •

The next night, the count was twelve.

Frank did not touch the pack at first. He stood at the cupboard with the door open and read the label from where he was. Mallory, V. Morphine sulphate 10 mg. Twelve in the cells, and the register said nine. He had written nine himself, in ink, twenty-four hours before.

He checked the lanyard. The key sat against his sternum, on its steel ring, where it had sat all shift. He had not taken it off to eat. He had not taken it off to use the toilet.

The following night it was thirteen. The night after that, fourteen.

On the Thursday morning he rang Elsie Ebdon at home. She answered on the fifth ring, with a radio going behind her.

"Frank. You're meant to be asleep."

"Elsie, who else has a key to the CD cupboard?"

"Me. You. That's the list, love. You know that." A kettle clicked off. "Why?"

"There's a pack in there that's gaining tablets."

She laughed. It was a warm, easy laugh, and it made him feel foolish. "Gaining. Frank. It's a stock transfer. We took that batch from the Alder Street branch in the spring, and somebody will have booked half of it in twice. I'll look at it Monday."

"The label's six years old."

"Then somebody's reused a card. Go home. Eat something."

She rang off. Frank stood in his kitchen with the phone in his hand. Elsie had not asked which pack. He had not told her.

That night he came in at nine and went straight to the dispensing bench. He tore a sheet from the A4 pad, laid it flat, and set the pack on top of it. Then he drew round the blister card with a pencil, cell by cell. Fourteen tablets, fourteen small circles, each one shaded in. The empty cells he left clear. He wrote the time in the corner. 9.20 p.m. He put the sheet and the pack back in the cupboard, turned the key, and hung the lanyard round his neck.

He did not sit down all night. He answered the hatch twice. He filled a methadone script for a man who called him "chief" and smelled of wet dog. At every hour he went to the cupboard door and stood with his hand flat against the steel, listening. There was nothing to hear. The fridge hummed.

At 2 a.m. he took the pack out and laid it on the sheet.

It fitted the pencil lines exactly. Fourteen shaded circles, fourteen tablets. Then he saw the fifteenth.

It sat in a cell he had drawn clear. He had left that circle white, and there it was, filled, white on white. He picked the pack up and tilted it under the lamp. The tablet was ordinary in shape. But the stamp on its face had gone. The letters had been rubbed smooth, the way a coin goes in a pocket, or a step goes under a thousand shoes.

Frank turned it over. The back was worn the same.

Somebody had held this a very long time.

• • •

Frank put the tablet down on the sheet, on its pencil circle, and did not touch it again.

The dead-records room was a cupboard behind the consulting booth. It smelled of toner and old carpet. He took the lamp in there with him and pulled the lever-arch files for the year in question. Six years back. The prescription had a number on the pack label, and the number led him to a green box file marked UNCOLLECTED, with a rubber band gone brittle round it.

The script was on top. He read it standing up.

Victor Mallory. Morphine sulphate, 10 mg, one tablet every twelve hours for seven days. Fourteen tablets in all. The prescriber's stamp was from the hospice. Under the patient's name, in the address box, someone had written: Night Caretaker's Flat, Beaumont Row.

Frank read that line twice.

Beaumont Row was this building. The pharmacy took the ground floor. The flat was above it, and had been empty since before he started.

The date on the script was a Tuesday. He remembered nothing of it, and that bothered him. He remembered most things. Under the script, folded small, was a death notice cut from the parish bulletin. Victor Mallory, aged sixty-eight, for eleven years night caretaker at Beaumont Row. Died on the Friday of that week. Someone had pinned it to the script with a staple, and the staple had rusted a brown ghost onto both pages.

He went back to the bench and laid the pack beside the script. He worked it through with a pencil. The course began with two tablets a day. The pack had given him one, then two, then a pair on the second night. The pack was not growing at random. It was keeping to the script, dose by dose, and in the right cells.

Fifteen tablets. Day eight of fourteen would be next.

He rang Elsie at ten to three. She picked up on the sixth ring, thick with sleep.

"Frank? What's happened?"

"Nothing's happened. I need to ask you something. Who cleared out the old basement dispensary, when the building was refitted?"

There was a long gap on the line. He could hear her breathing. Then a lighter click, though she had given up smoking years ago.

"Why do you want to know that?"

"Because Victor Mallory lived upstairs. You must have known him."

"I didn't." She said it flatly. "Frank, I've managed this branch eleven years. I've signed every day sheet in that drawer. I have never once seen Mr Mallory's name on one."

"Then he wasn't on days."

"No. He's on the night ones." Another pause. "In a hand that isn't mine, Frank. Or yours. I always took it for the locum's."

Frank looked at the night register, shut on the bench under the lamp.

"Elsie," he said, "what does the hand look like?"

She did not answer. Behind him, very faintly, the cupboard door ticked against its frame.

• • •

"What does it look like?" Frank said again.

"I'm not doing this at three in the morning," said Elsie. "Go home. Leave the cupboard."

"I can't leave it. I'm the one who's on."

She put the phone down. He heard the line click and then go flat.

He took the night register from the bench and opened it under the lamp. It was the long ledger with the green spine. Each night had a row. Date, opening count, closing count, signature of pharmacist, signature of checker. He turned back through it. Last week. Last month. Last year.

His own name sat in the pharmacist column, night after night, in blue ink. In the column beside it, the checker's column, there was a second hand. Small and upright. The pencil had been pressed hard enough to dent the page.

V. Mallory.

He had never worked with a checker. Nobody had. The pharmacy ran one person on nights, and he had always taken the second signature to be a formality that the system filled in. He had never looked at it.

He went back further. Two years. Four. Six. The hand did not change. V. Mallory, on every one of his shifts, from the first night he had ever been given the keys.

Frank took the sheet with the pack's cells drawn on it and laid it open on the register. Then he turned to the last page of the book, where the checker had a margin for notes. There were pencil lines there. Ruled boxes in rows of fourteen. Dots in some of them, none in others.

He held the sheet beside the margin. The dots matched. Every one he had pencilled, in the same cells, in the same order, and three that he had not drawn yet.

He sat for a while. The lamp hummed. Out in the shop the fridge cycled on.

Then he understood it, and it was plainer than he wanted. The pack was not filling. It had never been filling. Somebody had dispensed a course six years ago and it had never been handed over, so the count could not close. The tablets were not arriving. They were being brought back, one at a time, to the only person who stood at that cupboard every night.

He picked the pack up from the bench, where it had lain beside the script, and put it in the cupboard. He turned the key, and it turned easily. Then he took it out again and held it in his palm. The foil over the ninth cell was bulged, a little more than before.

In the drawer under the bench was the collection slip, still clipped to the script, the box at the bottom blank for six years. He took his pen. His hand was steady, which surprised him.

"If I sign," he said, to the empty shop, "it's closed."

Nothing answered.

He wrote: received, F. Farnsworth, 3.05 a.m. Then he signed his name under it and pressed the pen down hard.

The cupboard door, which he had left open, swung slowly shut behind him.

• • •

The shop was very quiet after that.

Frank stood with the pack in his hand and listened. The fridge had cycled off. The lamp had stopped humming, or he had stopped hearing it. He went to the register on the bench and opened it to the night's page. His own handwriting sat above the line. It gave the count of nine. Beneath it, in pencil that was not his, was the count of eleven, struck through. Then twelve. Then the figure he had been dreading, and it stood there plain. Fourteen. A full course, and the line ruled off beneath it.

It balanced. He had wanted that for four nights, and now he had it, and he did not want it at all.

He looked at the clock over the door. Three-oh-six.

"That's that," he said. His voice sounded thin in the room. "It's closed."

Nobody answered. He walked the pack back to the cupboard. The door had shut itself. He took the lanyard from his neck and found the key, and he turned the key, and the door opened with its usual small complaint. He raised the pack to the shelf.

Then he read the label. He had not read it again since the slip. There had been no need.

The printing was the same plain black. The pharmacy name, Beaumont Row. The drug, the strength, the quantity of fourteen. But the name above it had changed. It said Farnsworth, Frank. Beneath that was his date of birth, correct to the day. The instructions were the old instructions, one tablet every twelve hours. And at the bottom, where a dispenser prints the start of a course, it gave tomorrow's date.

He did not shout. He would have liked to say he did. He stood there with the pack at shoulder height and read it twice, because he could not believe a printer had done it, and there was no printer in the cupboard. Then he closed the door on it, and locked it, and put the key back inside his collar.

He thought of calling Elsie. He thought of the telephone and her voice going quiet. He did not call. What would he have said to her? That he had signed? She would only have told him what he already knew, that nobody else had.

The door was open again.

It had swung out an inch, and the pack lay on the shelf where he had not put it, label outward. He took it out. He did not remember deciding to. He carried it to the dispensing bench and sat down on the stool, the one with the torn vinyl, which Victor Mallory must have sat on for six years of nights. It was still warm.

The foil on the first cell had bulged. It strained very slightly, as though something were pressing from beneath, patient and polite. He slid his thumbnail under the edge and tore it back.

It came out into his open palm without being shaken. One small white tablet. He turned his hand to the lamp. The stamp on it was worn clean away, smooth as a pebble from a river, as if a great many hands had held it before his.

Behind him, in the dark of the shop, the cupboard key turned in the lock.

item.title: The Ash-Tree
item.description: In a damp Suffolk country house, a condemned woman whispers a promise on the gallows, and an old ash-tree keeps its own counsel beneath the moon. When the squire is found dead and blackened, something far stranger than poison may be at work.
item.content:encoded:
Everyone who has travelled over Eastern England knows the smaller country-houses with which it is studded—the rather dank little buildings, usually in the Italian style, surrounded with parks of some eighty to a hundred acres. For me they have always had a very strong attraction: with the grey paling of split oak, the noble trees, the meres with their reed-beds, and the line of distant woods. Then, I like the pillared portico—perhaps stuck on to a red-brick Queen Anne house which has been faced with stucco to bring it into line with the “Grecian” taste of the end of the eighteenth century; the hall inside, going up to the roof, which hall ought always to be provided with a gallery and a small organ. I like the library, too, where you may find anything from a Psalter of the thirteenth century to a Shakespeare quarto. I like the pictures, of course; and perhaps most of all I like fancying what life in such a house was when it was first built, and in the piping times of landlords’ prosperity, and not least now, when, if money is not so plentiful, taste is more varied and life quite as interesting. I wish to have one of these houses, and enough money to keep it together and entertain my friends in it modestly.

But this is a digression. I have to tell you of a curious series of events which happened in such a house as I have tried to describe. It is Castringham Hall in Suffolk. I think a good deal has been done to the building since the period of my story, but the essential features I have sketched are still there—Italian portico, square block of white house, older inside than out, park with fringe of woods, and mere. The one feature that marked out the house from a score of others is gone. As you looked at it from the park, you saw on the right a great old ash-tree growing within half a dozen yards of the wall, and almost or quite touching the building with its branches. I suppose it had stood there ever since Castringham ceased to be a fortified place, and since the moat was filled in and the Elizabethan dwelling-house built. At any rate, it had well-nigh attained its full dimensions in the year 1690.

In that year the district in which the Hall is situated was the scene of a number of witch-trials. It will be long, I think, before we arrive at a just estimate of the amount of solid reason—if there was any—which lay at the root of the universal fear of witches in old times. Whether the persons accused of this offence really did imagine that they were possessed of unusual power of any kind; or whether they had the will at least, if not the power, of doing mischief to their neighbours; or whether all the confessions, of which there are so many, were extorted by the mere cruelty of the witch-finders—these are questions which are not, I fancy, yet solved. And the present narrative gives me pause. I cannot altogether sweep it away as mere invention. The reader must judge for himself.

Castringham contributed a victim to the auto-da-fé. Mrs Mothersole was her name, and she differed from the ordinary run of village witches only in being rather better off and in a more influential position. Efforts were made to save her by several reputable farmers of the parish. They did their best to testify to her character, and showed considerable anxiety as to the verdict of the jury.

But what seems to have been fatal to the woman was the evidence of the then proprietor of Castringham Hall—Sir Matthew Fell. He deposed to having watched her on three different occasions from his window, at the full of the moon, gathering sprigs “from the ash-tree near my house”. She had climbed into the branches, clad only in her shift, and was cutting off small twigs with a peculiarly curved knife, and as she did so she seemed to be talking to herself. On each occasion Sir Matthew had done his best to capture the woman, but she had always taken alarm at some accidental noise he had made, and all he could see when he got down to the garden was a hare running across the path in the direction of the village.

On the third night he had been at the pains to follow at his best speed, and had gone straight to Mrs Mothersole’s house; but he had had to wait a quarter of an hour battering at her door, and then she had come out very cross, and apparently very sleepy, as if just out of bed; and he had no good explanation to offer of his visit.

Mainly on this evidence, though there was much more of a less striking and unusual kind from other parishioners, Mrs Mothersole was found guilty and condemned to die. She was hanged a week after the trial, with five or six more unhappy creatures, at Bury St Edmunds.

Sir Matthew Fell, then Deputy-Sheriff, was present at the execution. It was a damp, drizzly March morning when the cart made its way up the rough grass hill outside Northgate, where the gallows stood. The other victims were apathetic or broken down with misery; but Mrs Mothersole was, as in life so in death, of a very different temper. Her “poysonous Rage”, as a reporter of the time puts it, “did so work upon the Bystanders—yea, even upon the Hangman—that it was constantly affirmed of all that saw her that she presented the living Aspect of a mad Divell. Yet she offer’d no Resistance to the Officers of the Law; onely she looked upon those that laid Hands upon her with so direfull and venomous an Aspect that—as one of them afterwards assured me—the meer Thought of it preyed inwardly upon his Mind for six Months after.”

However, all that she is reported to have said was the seemingly meaningless words: “There will be guests at the Hall.” Which she repeated more than once in an undertone.

Sir Matthew Fell was not unimpressed by the bearing of the woman. He had some talk upon the matter with the Vicar of his parish, with whom he travelled home after the assize business was over. His evidence at the trial had not been very willingly given; he was not specially infected with the witch-finding mania, but he declared, then and afterwards, that he could not give any other account of the matter than that he had given, and that he could not possibly have been mistaken as to what he saw. The whole transaction had been repugnant to him, for he was a man who liked to be on pleasant terms with those about him; but he saw a duty to be done in this business, and he had done it. That seems to have been the gist of his sentiments, and the Vicar applauded it, as any reasonable man must have done.

• • •

A few weeks after, when the moon of May was at the full, Vicar and Squire met again in the park, and walked to the Hall together. Lady Fell was with her mother, who was dangerously ill, and Sir Matthew was alone at home; so the Vicar, Mr Crome, was easily persuaded to take a late supper at the Hall.

Sir Matthew was not very good company this evening. The talk ran chiefly on family and parish matters, and, as luck would have it, Sir Matthew made a memorandum in writing of certain wishes or intentions of his regarding his estates, which afterwards proved exceedingly useful.

When Mr Crome thought of starting for home, about half past nine o’clock, Sir Matthew and he took a preliminary turn on the gravelled walk at the back of the house. The only incident that struck Mr Crome was this: they were in sight of the ash-tree which I described as growing near the windows of the building, when Sir Matthew stopped and said:

“What is that that runs up and down the stem of the ash? It is never a squirrel? They will all be in their nests by now.”

The Vicar looked and saw the moving creature, but he could make nothing of its colour in the moonlight. The sharp outline, however, seen for an instant, was imprinted on his brain, and he could have sworn, he said, though it sounded foolish, that, squirrel or not, it had more than four legs.

Still, not much was to be made of the momentary vision, and the two men parted. They may have met since then, but it was not for a score of years.

Next day Sir Matthew Fell was not downstairs at six in the morning, as was his custom, nor at seven, nor yet at eight. Hereupon the servants went and knocked at his chamber door. I need not prolong the description of their anxious listenings and renewed batterings on the panels. The door was opened at last from the outside, and they found their master dead and black. So much you have guessed. That there were any marks of violence did not at the moment appear; but the window was open.

One of the men went to fetch the parson, and then by his directions rode on to give notice to the coroner. Mr Crome himself went as quick as he might to the Hall, and was shown to the room where the dead man lay. He has left some notes among his papers which show how genuine a respect and sorrow was felt for Sir Matthew, and there is also this passage, which I transcribe for the sake of the light it throws upon the course of events, and also upon the common beliefs of the time:

“There was not any the least Trace of an Entrance having been forc’d to the Chamber: but the Casement stood open, as my poor Friend would always have it in this Season. He had his Evening Drink of small Ale in a silver vessel of about a pint measure, and tonight had not drunk it out. This Drink was examined by the Physician from Bury, a Mr Hodgkins, who could not, however, as he afterwards declar’d upon his Oath, before the Coroner’s quest, discover that any matter of a venomous kind was present in it. For, as was natural, in the great Swelling and Blackness of the Corpse, there was talk made among the Neighbours of Poyson. The Body was very much Disorder’d as it laid in the Bed, being twisted after so extream a sort as gave too probable Conjecture that my worthy Friend and Patron had expir’d in great Pain and Agony. And what is as yet unexplain’d, and to myself the Argument of some Horrid and Artfull Designe in the Perpetrators of this Barbarous Murther, was this, that the Women which were entrusted with the laying-out of the Corpse and washing it, being both sad Persons and very well Respected in their Mournfull Profession, came to me in a great Pain and Distress both of Mind and Body, saying, what was indeed confirmed upon the first View, that they had no sooner touch’d the Breast of the Corpse with their naked Hands than they were sensible of a more than ordinary violent Smart and Acheing in their Palms, which, with their whole Forearms, in no long time swell’d so immoderately, the Pain still continuing, that, as afterwards proved, during many weeks they were forc’d to lay by the exercise of their Calling; and yet no mark seen on the Skin.

“Upon hearing this, I sent for the Physician, who was still in the House, and we made as carefull a Proof as we were able by the Help of a small Magnifying Lens of Crystal of the condition of the Skinn on this Part of the Body: but could not detect with the Instrument we had any Matter of Importance beyond a couple of small Punctures or Pricks, which we then concluded were the Spotts by which the Poyson might be introduced, remembering that Ring of Pope Borgia, with other known Specimens of the Horrid Art of the Italian Poysoners of the last age.

“So much is to be said of the Symptoms seen on the Corpse. As to what I am to add, it is meerly my own Experiment, and to be left to Posterity to judge whether there be anything of Value therein. There was on the Table by the Beddside a Bible of the small size, in which my Friend—punctuall as in Matters of less Moment, so in this more weighty one—used nightly, and upon his First Rising, to read a sett Portion. And I taking it up—not without a Tear duly paid to him wich from the Study of this poorer Adumbration was now pass’d to the contemplation of its great Originall—it came into my Thoughts, as at such moments of Helplessness we are prone to catch at any the least Glimmer that makes promise of Light, to make trial of that old and by many accounted Superstitious Practice of drawing the Sortes; of which a Principall Instance, in the case of his late Sacred Majesty the Blessed Martyr King Charles and my Lord Falkland, was now much talked of. I must needs admit that by my Trial not much Assistance was afforded me: yet, as the Cause and Origin of these Dreadfull Events may hereafter be search’d out, I set down the Results, in the case it may be found that they pointed the true Quarter of the Mischief to a quicker Intelligence than my own.

• • •

“I made, then, three trials, opening the Book and placing my Finger upon certain Words: which gave in the first these words, from Luke xiii. 7, Cut it down; in the second, Isaiah xiii. 20, It shall never be inhabited; and upon the third Experiment, Job xxxix. 30, Her young ones also suck up blood.”

This is all that need be quoted from Mr Crome’s papers. Sir Matthew Fell was duly coffined and laid into the earth, and his funeral sermon, preached by Mr Crome on the following Sunday, has been printed under the title of “The Unsearchable Way; or, England’s Danger and the Malicious Dealings of Antichrist”, it being the Vicar’s view, as well as that most commonly held in the neighbourhood, that the Squire was the victim of a recrudescence of the Popish Plot.

His son, Sir Matthew the second, succeeded to the title and estates. And so ends the first act of the Castringham tragedy. It is to be mentioned, though the fact is not surprising, that the new Baronet did not occupy the room in which his father had died. Nor, indeed, was it slept in by anyone but an occasional visitor during the whole of his occupation. He died in 1735, and I do not find that anything particular marked his reign, save a curiously constant mortality among his cattle and live-stock in general, which showed a tendency to increase slightly as time went on.

Those who are interested in the details will find a statistical account in a letter to the Gentleman’s Magazine of 1772, which draws the facts from the Baronet’s own papers. He put an end to it at last by a very simple expedient, that of shutting up all his beasts in sheds at night, and keeping no sheep in his park. For he had noticed that nothing was ever attacked that spent the night indoors. After that the disorder confined itself to wild birds, and beasts of chase. But as we have no good account of the symptoms, and as all-night watching was quite unproductive of any clue, I do not dwell on what the Suffolk farmers called the “Castringham sickness”.

The second Sir Matthew died in 1735, as I said, and was duly succeeded by his son, Sir Richard. It was in his time that the great family pew was built out on the north side of the parish church. So large were the Squire’s ideas that several of the graves on that unhallowed side of the building had to be disturbed to satisfy his requirements. Among them was that of Mrs Mothersole, the position of which was accurately known, thanks to a note on a plan of the church and yard, both made by Mr Crome.

A certain amount of interest was excited in the village when it was known that the famous witch, who was still remembered by a few, was to be exhumed. And the feeling of surprise, and indeed disquiet, was very strong when it was found that, though her coffin was fairly sound and unbroken, there was no trace whatever inside it of body, bones, or dust. Indeed, it is a curious phenomenon, for at the time of her burying no such things were dreamt of as resurrection-men, and it is difficult to conceive any rational motive for stealing a body otherwise than for the uses of the dissecting-room.

The incident revived for a time all the stories of witch-trials and of the exploits of the witches, dormant for forty years, and Sir Richard’s orders that the coffin should be burnt were thought by a good many to be rather foolhardy, though they were duly carried out.

Sir Richard was a pestilent innovator, it is certain. Before his time the Hall had been a fine block of the mellowest red brick; but Sir Richard had travelled in Italy and become infected with the Italian taste, and, having more money than his predecessors, he determined to leave an Italian palace where he had found an English house. So stucco and ashlar masked the brick; some indifferent Roman marbles were planted about in the entrance-hall and gardens; a reproduction of the Sibyl’s temple at Tivoli was erected on the opposite bank of the mere; and Castringham took on an entirely new, and, I must say, a less engaging, aspect. But it was much admired, and served as a model to a good many of the neighbouring gentry in after-years.

One morning (it was in 1754) Sir Richard woke after a night of discomfort. It had been windy, and his chimney had smoked persistently, and yet it was so cold that he must keep up a fire. Also something had so rattled about the window that no man could get a moment’s peace. Further, there was the prospect of several guests of position arriving in the course of the day, who would expect sport of some kind, and the inroads of the distemper (which continued among his game) had been lately so serious that he was afraid for his reputation as a game-preserver. But what really touched him most nearly was the other matter of his sleepless night. He could certainly not sleep in that room again.

That was the chief subject of his meditations at breakfast, and after it he began a systematic examination of the rooms to see which would suit his notions best. It was long before he found one. This had a window with an eastern aspect and that with a northern; this door the servants would be always passing, and he did not like the bedstead in that. No, he must have a room with a western look-out, so that the sun could not wake him early, and it must be out of the way of the business of the house. The housekeeper was at the end of her resources.

• • •

“Well, Sir Richard,” she said, “you know that there is but the one room like that in the house.”

“Which may that be?” said Sir Richard.

“And that is Sir Matthew’s—the West Chamber.”

“Well, put me in there, for there I’ll lie tonight,” said her master. “Which way is it? Here, to be sure;” and he hurried off.

“Oh, Sir Richard, but no one has slept there these forty years. The air has hardly been changed since Sir Matthew died there.”

Thus she spoke, and rustled after him.

“Come, open the door, Mrs Chiddock. I’ll see the chamber, at least.”

So it was opened, and, indeed, the smell was very close and earthy. Sir Richard crossed to the window, and, impatiently, as was his wont, threw the shutters back, and flung open the casement. For this end of the house was one which the alterations had barely touched, grown up as it was with the great ash-tree, and being otherwise concealed from view.

“Air it, Mrs Chiddock, all today, and move my bed-furniture in in the afternoon. Put the Bishop of Kilmore in my old room.”

“Pray, Sir Richard,” said a new voice, breaking in on this speech, “might I have the favour of a moment’s interview?”

Sir Richard turned round and saw a man in black in the doorway, who bowed.

“I must ask your indulgence for this intrusion, Sir Richard. You will, perhaps, hardly remember me. My name is William Crome, and my grandfather was Vicar here in your grandfather’s time.”

“Well, sir,” said Sir Richard, “the name of Crome is always a passport to Castringham. I am glad to renew a friendship of two generations” standing. In what can I serve you? for your hour of calling—and, if I do not mistake you, your bearing—shows you to be in some haste.”

“That is no more than the truth, sir. I am riding from Norwich to Bury St Edmunds with what haste I can make, and I have called in on my way to leave with you some papers which we have but just come upon in looking over what my grandfather left at his death. It is thought you may find some matters of family interest in them.”

“You are mighty obliging, Mr Crome, and, if you will be so good as to follow me to the parlour, and drink a glass of wine, we will take a first look at these same papers together. And you, Mrs Chiddock, as I said, be about airing this chamber…. Yes, it is here my grandfather died…. Yes, the tree, perhaps, does make the place a little dampish…. No; I do not wish to listen to any more. Make no difficulties, I beg. You have your orders—go. Will you follow me, sir?”

They went to the study. The packet which young Mr Crome had brought—he was then just become a Fellow of Clare Hall in Cambridge, I may say, and subsequently brought out a respectable edition of Polyaenus—contained among other things the notes which the old Vicar had made upon the occasion of Sir Matthew Fell’s death. And for the first time Sir Richard was confronted with the enigmatical Sortes Biblicæ which you have heard. They amused him a good deal.

“Well,” he said, “my grandfather’s Bible gave one prudent piece of advice—Cut it down. If that stands for the ash-tree, he may rest assured I shall not neglect it. Such a nest of catarrhs and agues was never seen.”

The parlour contained the family books, which, pending the arrival of a collection which Sir Richard had made in Italy, and the building of a proper room to receive them, were not many in number.

Sir Richard looked up from the paper to the bookcase.

“I wonder,” says he, “whether the old prophet is there yet? I fancy I see him.”

Crossing the room, he took out a dumpy Bible, which, sure enough, bore on the flyleaf the inscription: “To Matthew Fell, from his Loving Godmother, Anne Aldous, 2 September, 1659.”

“It would be no bad plan to test him again, Mr Crome. I will wager we get a couple of names in the Chronicles. H’m! what have we here? ‘Thou shalt seek me in the morning, and I shall not be.’ Well, well! Your grandfather would have made a fine omen of that, hey? No more prophets for me! They are all in a tale. And now, Mr Crome, I am infinitely obliged to you for your packet. You will, I fear, be impatient to get on. Pray allow me—another glass.”

So with offers of hospitality, which were genuinely meant (for Sir Richard thought well of the young man’s address and manner), they parted.

In the afternoon came the guests—the Bishop of Kilmore, Lady Mary Hervey, Sir William Kentfield, etc. Dinner at five, wine, cards, supper, and dispersal to bed.

Next morning Sir Richard is disinclined to take his gun with the rest. He talks with the Bishop of Kilmore. This prelate, unlike a good many of the Irish Bishops of his day, had visited his see, and, indeed, resided there, for some considerable time. This morning, as the two were walking along the terrace and talking over the alterations and improvements in the house, the Bishop said, pointing to the window of the West Room:

“You could never get one of my Irish flock to occupy that room, Sir Richard.”

“Why is that, my lord? It is, in fact, my own.”

“Well, our Irish peasantry will always have it that it brings the worst of luck to sleep near an ash-tree, and you have a fine growth of ash not two yards from your chamber window. Perhaps,” the Bishop went on, with a smile, “it has given you a touch of its quality already, for you do not seem, if I may say it, so much the fresher for your night’s rest as your friends would like to see you.”

“That, or something else, it is true, cost me my sleep from twelve to four, my lord. But the tree is to come down tomorrow, so I shall not hear much more from it.”

“I applaud your determination. It can hardly be wholesome to have the air you breathe strained, as it were, through all that leafage.”

• • •

“Your lordship is right there, I think. But I had not my window open last night. It was rather the noise that went on—no doubt from the twigs sweeping the glass—that kept me open-eyed.”

“I think that can hardly be, Sir Richard. Here—you see it from this point. None of these nearest branches even can touch your casement unless there were a gale, and there was none of that last night. They miss the panes by a foot.”

“No, sir, true. What, then, will it be, I wonder, that scratched and rustled so—ay, and covered the dust on my sill with lines and marks?”

At last they agreed that the rats must have come up through the ivy. That was the Bishop’s idea, and Sir Richard jumped at it.

So the day passed quietly, and night came, and the party dispersed to their rooms, and wished Sir Richard a better night.

And now we are in his bedroom, with the light out and the Squire in bed. The room is over the kitchen, and the night outside still and warm, so the window stands open.

There is very little light about the bedstead, but there is a strange movement there; it seems as if Sir Richard were moving his head rapidly to and fro with only the slightest possible sound. And now you would guess, so deceptive is the half-darkness, that he had several heads, round and brownish, which move back and forward, even as low as his chest. It is a horrible illusion. Is it nothing more? There! something drops off the bed with a soft plump, like a kitten, and is out of the window in a flash; another—four—and after that there is quiet again.

“Thou shalt seek me in the morning, and I shall not be.”

As with Sir Matthew, so with Sir Richard—dead and black in his bed!

A pale and silent party of guests and servants gathered under the window when the news was known. Italian poisoners, Popish emissaries, infected air—all these and more guesses were hazarded, and the Bishop of Kilmore looked at the tree, in the fork of whose lower boughs a white tom-cat was crouching, looking down the hollow which years had gnawed in the trunk. It was watching something inside the tree with great interest.

Suddenly it got up and craned over the hole. Then a bit of the edge on which it stood gave way, and it went slithering in. Everyone looked up at the noise of the fall.

It is known to most of us that a cat can cry; but few of us have heard, I hope, such a yell as came out of the trunk of the great ash. Two or three screams there were—the witnesses are not sure which—and then a slight and muffled noise of some commotion or struggling was all that came. But Lady Mary Hervey fainted outright, and the housekeeper stopped her ears and fled till she fell on the terrace.

The Bishop of Kilmore and Sir William Kentfield stayed. Yet even they were daunted, though it was only at the cry of a cat; and Sir William swallowed once or twice before he could say:

“There is something more than we know of in that tree, my lord. I am for an instant search.”

And this was agreed upon. A ladder was brought, and one of the gardeners went up, and, looking down the hollow, could detect nothing but a few dim indications of something moving. They got a lantern, and let it down by a rope.

“We must get at the bottom of this. My life upon it, my lord, but the secret of these terrible deaths is there.”

Up went the gardener again with the lantern, and let it down the hole cautiously. They saw the yellow light upon his face as he bent over, and saw his face struck with an incredulous terror and loathing before he cried out in a dreadful voice and fell back from the ladder—where, happily, he was caught by two of the men—letting the lantern fall inside the tree.

He was in a dead faint, and it was some time before any word could be got from him.

By then they had something else to look at. The lantern must have broken at the bottom, and the light in it caught upon dry leaves and rubbish that lay there, for in a few minutes a dense smoke began to come up, and then flame; and, to be short, the tree was in a blaze.

The bystanders made a ring at some yards’ distance, and Sir William and the Bishop sent men to get what weapons and tools they could; for, clearly, whatever might be using the tree as its lair would be forced out by the fire.

So it was. First, at the fork, they saw a round body covered with fire—the size of a man’s head—appear very suddenly, then seem to collapse and fall back. This, five or six times; then a similar ball leapt into the air and fell on the grass, where after a moment it lay still. The Bishop went as near as he dared to it, and saw—what but the remains of an enormous spider, veinous and seared! And, as the fire burned lower down, more terrible bodies like this began to break out from the trunk, and it was seen that these were covered with greyish hair.

All that day the ash burned, and until it fell to pieces the men stood about it, and from time to time killed the brutes as they darted out. At last there was a long interval when none appeared, and they cautiously closed in and examined the roots of the tree.

“They found,” says the Bishop of Kilmore, “below it a rounded hollow place in the earth, wherein were two or three bodies of these creatures that had plainly been smothered by the smoke; and, what is to me more curious, at the side of this den, against the wall, was crouching the anatomy or skeleton of a human being, with the skin dried upon the bones, having some remains of black hair, which was pronounced by those that examined it to be undoubtedly the body of a woman, and clearly dead for a period of fifty years.”

item.title: The Greywell Ledger
item.description: A records clerk receives an unmarked parcel containing a small walnut television that glows only in the dark, and what it shows is her own stairwell. Each night the picture runs a little longer, and the woman on the screen looks more and more like someone she knows.
item.content:encoded:
The parcel was on the doormat when I came up from the street on Tuesday evening. It was the first week of November, and it had rained since dawn. The stairwell of the Greywell smelled of wet coats and boiled cabbage, as it always did in that month.

I live on the fourth floor. There is no lift. I had climbed all four flights with my umbrella dripping on every landing, and I was in no humour for a puzzle.

The parcel was the size of a hatbox, wrapped in brown paper and tied with garden twine. The knot was an old one, a sailor's knot, pulled very tight. My name was on the label in ink: Miss A. Farrow, Flat 4C, the Greywell, Calder Street. There was no stamp and no postmark. There was no sender.

I stood there a while with my key in my hand. Then I carried it in.

I am a records clerk at the Records Office. I spend my days checking that one piece of paper agrees with another. So I did what I would have done at work. I set the parcel on the kitchen table and looked for the order that explained it. I had no order. I had bought nothing in a month except stockings.

I cut the twine with the bread knife. Under the paper was a box of plain deal, and under the lid, packed in shavings, was a television.

It was a small one. I would say the screen was no wider than my two hands laid side by side. The case was walnut, worn pale at the corners, and the glass was dark and slightly convex. There were two brass knobs and no names on either. I turned the set over. There was no flex at the back and no socket for one. I looked for a battery door and found none.

I said, aloud, "Well, that's no use to anybody."

My voice sounded foolish in the kitchen. I put the set on the chest of drawers in my bedroom, because that was the only clear surface. Then I ate my supper, washed the plate and read the evening paper to the end. I did not think about the parcel again. I want that understood. I was not uneasy.

At ten I went round the flat and put out the lamps. Kitchen first, then the sitting room. Last, the little brass lamp beside my bed. I lay down. The rain was loud on the sash.

Something was wrong with the dark. It took me a moment to see what. It had a pale patch in it, low and square, on the far side of the room.

I sat up. The television was lit.

There was no hum. There was no click. The glass glowed a dull silver, and in it, small and clear, a woman was climbing a stair. She wore a coat and carried nothing. She went up slowly, one hand on the rail. At each landing she stopped and looked up the well, as if counting.

The rail was iron, with a brass cap at the turn. The fourth step from the top was chipped on its nosing, and the wall beside it was painted the green that the landlord had chosen in 1949 and never replaced.

I knew that stair. I had climbed it that evening, with a dripping umbrella.

The woman reached my landing, and turned towards my door.

• • •

I did not open the door. I sat on the edge of the bed and watched the woman on the glass stand outside it, one hand raised, not knocking. Then the picture closed up to a point and was gone. The room was only a room again. I counted to a hundred before I put on the lamp.

On Wednesday I came home at six with a torch from the hall cupboard, a candle and a box of matches. I meant to be methodical. I am a records clerk. It is what I do with anything that frightens me.

I turned out the lamps at ten, and lay with the torch beside me. Nothing. I lay there twenty minutes. Then I switched the torch on, just to see my hand, and the set was already lit. It had not waited for me to turn the torch off. It had waited for me to stop looking at the room, or the room had stopped being dark enough to forbid it. I did not know which. I switched the torch off, and the woman was on the stair again, a little further along.

On Thursday I lit the candle and put it on the sill, and the glass stayed blank. I drew the curtain across the candle. Still blank. I blew it out, and the picture came. I wrote the times in the back of my diary. Wednesday ran four minutes. Thursday ran seven.

On Friday I hung a blanket over the curtain rail, to be certain of the dark, and I sat up in bed with the diary on my knee. It ran eleven minutes. This time the stair gave way to a street, wet and lamplit, and I knew it by the third frame. Calder Street. The Greywell's own railings, then the chemist's, then the post box with the chipped crown.

Between the chemist's and the corner there was a shopfront I could not place. A narrow window. Gilt lettering, too small to read. A blind half down.

Someone knocked at the door.

I put on the lamp, and the glass went out at once. Stanley Ingram stood on the landing in his slippers, with his keys on their ring in his hand. He is sixty or so, and slow, and he has kept the Greywell for as long as I have lived in it.

"Miss Farrow. I'm sorry. There's a noise coming through the ceiling of three. A sort of hum."

"There's no hum," I said. "It doesn't make one."

He looked past me at the bedroom door. I do not know why I said it. "I've been sent a television. I never ordered it."

"A television." He frowned. "Let's have a look."

He stood in the doorway a long while. He did not go near it. "It isn't on the inventory," he said at last. "I have the list of every set in this building, going back to the first owner. Lodgers' wireless sets, the lot. There's no walnut one. And no plug."

"I know."

"Nobody's got one like that, Miss Farrow."

I made him sit down. I told him what I had seen that night, leaving out the stair. I said only that it showed Calder Street, and a shop between the chemist's and the corner.

"Gilt lettering?" he said. "Blind half down?"

"Yes."

He took off his cap and turned it round in his hands. "That was Pell's, the clockmaker. It shut in 1961. It's been a bank for thirty years."

I looked at him.

"Which way was the blind?" he said.

• • •

"Which way was the blind?" Stanley had said, and I had told him. Half down, I said. Pulled to the left, as if someone had meant to finish the job and been called away.

He nodded slowly and put his cap back on. He said he would sleep better not knowing why I asked. Then he went down the stair, and I heard him stop twice on the way.

That was the fourth night. By the fifth I had stopped pretending it was a fault in the wiring.

On the fifth night I sat on the bedroom floor with my back against the wardrobe and the pencil in my hand, and I put out the last lamp myself. The glass woke at once. The woman was on the stair again, the fourth-floor stair of the Greywell, with its brass rod missing at the turn. She came down into the light of the landing window and I saw her face.

It was mine. There was no doubt left to argue with. She wore the brown cardigan, the one with the leather button replaced by a black one. I had worn it that morning to the Records Office. I had hung it on the chair not two hours before.

She carried a suitcase. Her free hand held the rail. She did not hurry, and she did not look back at the flat.

I have never owned a suitcase. I had never once, in eleven years, thought of leaving.

I sat there until the picture went to snow, and then to black. I put the pencil down on the boards. I got up, found the telephone in the hall, and rang a number I had to look for in the back of my address book.

Horace Trevelyan answered on the ninth ring. He was eighty-one, and had handled the sale of the Greywell for the estate. I had met him exactly once, at a signing.

"Miss Farrow," he said. "It's gone midnight."

"I know. I'm sorry. I need to ask about a television."

There was a silence on the line. It was not the silence of a man who had to think.

"Walnut," he said. "Small. No flex."

"Yes."

"It came with the building. It was never in the schedule of fixtures, and I was told to leave it off." He cleared his throat. "The first owner left it. A Mrs Ingram. She lived on the fourth floor herself, as it happens. She told me once that it was the only honest record of the tenants."

"The tenants," I said.

"Her word. I took it for a joke."

"Mrs Ingram. Any relation to the caretaker?"

"I couldn't say. I never asked." Another pause. "She left in October of 1958. Walked out one night with a suitcase, past the porter, who wished her good evening. She wished him the same. Nobody saw her after that. Her rent was paid, you understand. Paid a good while ahead."

I looked down the hall at the bedroom door. It stood open, and the room beyond it was dark.

"Mr Trevelyan, was there a woman living here after she left? A woman who took her flat?"

He did not answer that. I heard him breathing.

"Miss Farrow," he said at last, very gently. "Which floor did you say you were on?"

• • •

"Fourth," I said. "The fourth floor."

"Yes," said Mr Trevelyan. "That's what I was afraid of."

He would say nothing more. He wished me goodnight, and he said it kindly, and the line went dead. I stood in the hall with the receiver in my hand. Then I put it down and went to the kitchen drawer for a pencil.

I found one, and a pad of the buff forms I brought home from the Records Office. I carried them to the armchair in the sitting room. I switched off the last lamp. The television woke at once, as it always did, with that low grain of light, and I sat in front of it with the pad on my knee.

I had decided on a method. I would not watch the story. I would copy it, frame by frame, as a clerk copies a register entry. Time, place, who was present, what each person carried. If it was a record, I could read it like one.

The woman on the screen came out of the front door of the Greywell at ten past six in the morning. Calder Street was wet. She had a suitcase. I wrote that down. She turned left, toward the tram stop, and a man with a milk crate stepped aside for her.

Then the picture cut to the same door, the same hour, the next day. A second woman came in from the street. She wore the brown cardigan. She had my face, my walk, even the small hitch in the left shoulder where I carry my bag. She nodded to the porter, and he nodded back. He did not look twice.

I wrote: *She is not followed. She is not stopped.*

The picture cut again. A different door, a different decade. I knew it by the lamp-brackets. A man in a belted overcoat carried a case out of the Greywell, and the next morning another man in a belted overcoat carried a case in. The same face. The same coat. A hat was lifted to the same porter.

I turned the page and kept writing. A girl with a hatbox. A widow, by her veiling. Each one went out at dawn, and each one was replaced. Nobody remarked on it. Nobody on that screen ever remarked on it.

My pencil had stopped. I looked at what I had written, and it was not a forecast. I saw that now. A forecast is a thing you can refuse. This was a ledger. These people had not been going to leave. They had left already, and the dark had only been showing me the entry.

I thought of Mrs Ingram, and her rent paid a good while ahead.

On the screen, the woman in my cardigan was back in my sitting room. I watched her cross it. She sat in my armchair. She put a pad on her knee, and she began to write. I watched her write for nearly a minute, and I could not read the page.

Then she stopped. She lifted her head, and she looked out of the glass at me. Slowly she turned and reached for the lamp on the side table. Her hand closed on the switch.

I knew what came next. She would put the light on. The set would go dark, and I would go to the bedroom and fetch my coat, and go. I had been going to do it. I could feel it, like a word on the tip of the tongue.

I did not move my hand toward the lamp.

I stood up instead. The pad slid to the carpet. I crossed the room in the dark, with the picture throwing my own shadow ahead of me, and I took my coat from the chair. It was the heavy tweed, the one I wear to the Records Office in winter. I held it up with both hands.

On the screen, the woman in the cardigan was holding up a coat as well.

I laid it over the glass.

The light went out of the room. There was no sound at all, and then, from beneath the tweed, very faintly, I heard something that was almost a knock.

• • •

I did not lift the coat until it was light.

I sat on the floor with my back against the armchair, the tweed held down with both hands, and I let the knocking stop of its own accord. It took some time. Towards five it grew weaker, like a clock running down. After that there was only the rain on the window, and the sound of my own breath.

At eight, someone knocked at the door itself. It was a plain knock, two raps, the knock of a man with a clipboard.

"Miss Farrow? It's Stanley Ingram."

I opened it on the chain. He stood on the landing in his brown overall, with the rent book under his arm, and he looked pleased, as a man does who brings good news.

"Thought you'd want to hear it from me," he said. "Your rent's been paid. A full year in advance, Miss Farrow, in cash, to the office this morning. I've never known the like."

"I haven't paid it," I said.

"No, no. The lady did." He smiled. "Brown cardigan. Very neat. She said you'd be tired, and I wasn't to disturb you till eight. She left something for you in the hall. I've carried it up."

He stepped aside. On the landing, against the banister, stood a suitcase. It was a leather case, old and square, with brass corners gone dull. The strap was buckled once, not twice.

"Did you see her face, Mr Ingram?"

He thought about it honestly. That was the worst of it. "Do you know," he said, "I couldn't tell you. But she knew the building. She never asked for the stairs."

He went down, whistling a little. I heard him reach the third floor, and the second, and then the street door, and then nothing.

I took off the chain. I knelt on the landing mat, where the parcel had lain in November, and I undid the strap. The lid was stiff. It came up with a small dry sound.

The television lay inside, packed in my own blue scarf. The walnut case was warm. I felt it through the wool before I touched it, as you feel a stone that has been in the sun. It was ten past eight on a bright wet morning, with the skylight over the stair full of daylight, and the glass was lit.

The picture was faint but quite plain. It showed a door, painted green, with a brass 4B above the letterbox. It was my door. It was empty on both sides, and the camera stood where I was kneeling now.

The door was opening.

I turned my head. Behind me, my own door stood shut, as I had left it. I looked back at the glass. The gap widened, an inch at a time, and in the gap there was a hand on the edge of the wood, in a brown cuff, with a pencil held between two fingers.

I could hear the latch behind me begin to turn.

item.title: The Fare to Nowhere
item.description: Every night the app freezes for four seconds, and every night a silent passenger sits a little closer to the driver's seat. Douglas Whitlow has a cold flask, a dead address, and a growing suspicion that his rider has never wanted to arrive.
item.content:encoded:
The request came in at twenty past eleven, on a wet Tuesday night in October, and I accepted it because I had been parked outside the Harcastle Co-operative for forty minutes with nothing but a cold flask for company. The pickup pin sat at the far end of Harcastle Road, where the street lamps give out and the road drops towards the railway cutting. I had never been given a fare there. The estimate was eleven minutes away.

I drove it in nine. The rain came in sideways off the allotments, and the wipers on my Skoda have never cleared more than the middle two-thirds of the glass. At the underpass I slowed, as I always do, because the road narrows there and the brick sweats. The work phone sat clamped in its mount on the dashboard, and the pin on its screen showed a blue dot, then a blue dot with a ring around it, then the word *Arriving*.

Then the screen froze.

I have driven for the app for three years and I know its habits. It stalls in the cutting and under the rail bridge; it stalls whenever a lorry parks too close to the mast on Fenner Lane. A frozen screen is nothing. The map goes grey, the little car stops turning, and the radio carries on without it. I put the handbrake on and counted, as one does. One. Two. The heater ticked. Three. Somewhere behind me a drainpipe was emptying itself onto the tarmac.

Four, and the display came back, and the rear door was shut.

I had not heard it open. I want to be exact about this. I heard no latch, no change in the weight of the car on its springs, no rush of rain. But the interior light was off, as I had left it, and in the mirror there was a man sitting directly behind me, hands folded on his knees, a hat on his lap.

"Good evening," he said. "I'm sorry to have kept you."

"Mr Drummond?" I said, because the app said so. *Harold D., 4.9 stars.* There was no photograph.

"That's right."

He was perhaps sixty. His face had the colour of wet slate, not ill, exactly, but finished with colour, and his raincoat was dry. I noticed that at once and decided not to notice it. The coat was of a cut my father wore. The hat on his knee was a flat cap, and it was dry as well.

"Where are we heading?"

He gave me an address: *Number nine, Wick Yard, off the Harcastle Road.* I typed it. The app considered it and returned a small red line of text. *Address not found.* I tried it without the number, then without the yard. Nothing. I said so, apologetically, and offered to use my own map.

"You won't need it," said Mr Drummond. "Keep to the road. I shall tell you." He settled back. "You mustn't mind the quiet, Mr Whitlow. I'm not much for conversation."

I had not told him my name. It was on the dashboard card, of course, in the little plastic window, and I told myself that.

I released the handbrake. The display was still lit, and in the corner, where the bars of signal should have been, there was a single grey dash. Beside it, in type too small to read, the app had begun to count something upwards.

In the mirror, Mr Drummond was sitting very still. It seemed to me that the back seat was a little narrower than it had been.

• • •

I drove on because there was nothing else to do. Mr Drummond named the turnings a half-second before I reached them, *left here, now the second right*, in a voice with no weight behind it, and at the end of Wick Yard there was no Number nine. There was a wall, a drain, and a sodium lamp that had been dead long enough to grow moss. I stopped. When I turned in my seat the back was empty, the leather dry, the cushion not even dented. The work phone gave three bars of signal and a rating request. I did not give one.

On Wednesday the account asked for me again.

*Harold D.* The pickup was the Harcastle Road underpass, where the concrete takes every bar from the screen, and I told myself I would cancel. My thumb was on the button when everything stopped. The picture did not go black. It held, bright and perfectly still, and the clock in the corner stopped at 22:41. I heard the rear door close. Nothing had opened it.

"Good evening, Mr Whitlow."

He sat behind the passenger headrest now, no longer in the middle. I could see the flat cap in the corner of the mirror, and one grey ear. "Mr Drummond," I said. "What is it you want? Where is it you want to go?" He said, "Keep to the road." The clock moved. 22:42. I drove him through four miles of wet streets that led, as before, to nothing. He spoke only to direct me. When I asked a third time what he wanted, he looked out of the window as a man does who has been asked something rude.

On Thursday I took the pickup in the car park behind the Harcastle Infirmary, which has been shuttered since the spring, with plywood across the casualty doors and a single fox watching me from the ambulance bay. I had decided to keep both hands on the wheel and not turn. The display froze again. I counted. At four seconds the cold arrived at my right shoulder, the way a draught arrives from a door you thought was shut, and a hand came down upon the console between the seats.

It was a large hand, grey as the face, the nails cut square. It lay beside the gear stick with the fingers a little spread, patient, exactly where a driver rests his own. There was a gold ring on it, worn thin. A faint smell came with it, and I knew it before I could name it: engine oil, and pipe tobacco, and the inside of an old coat.

"Mr Drummond," I said, and my voice did something I had not permitted it to do. "Please. What do you want?"

He did not answer. He was looking, I think, at the wheel. I could feel him looking at the place where my hands were.

The picture thawed. 23:17. A single bar of signal came back, and the app, with its usual cheerfulness, congratulated me on a ride completed.

The hand was still on the console. It stayed there for the whole drive home, and I did not once look down. When I parked outside Alder Close and switched off the engine, I sat a long minute listening to the rain, and then I heard the rear door open and close, quietly, and I understood that he had stepped out first.

• • •

I did not telephone anyone that night. I sat in the kitchen with the lights on and the back door locked and a cup of tea I never drank. At some point after two the cup was cold, and I found I had been watching the chair opposite me.

In the morning I rang the driver support line from the bottom of the garden, standing among the wet bean poles. It seemed to me that a thing which could follow a car might not follow a signal as far as a shed. I used the house phone, the cordless one, carried down the path with its aerial out. The work phone, the one that ran the app, I had left in my coat pocket on the hook by the shed door.

There was a menu. There was a recording that told me my call was important. After eleven minutes a young woman took my driver number and my name, asked me to describe the issue, and listened to the description with the courteous blankness of someone reading from a card. She said she would put me through to a supervisor. The line clicked twice.

"Hargreaves," said a man. "Vernon Hargreaves. Go ahead, Mr Whitlow."

His voice was flat and unhurried, a voice with the edges planed off. I told him everything: the Tuesday request, the four seconds, the man in the back, the three nights since, the hand on the console. I said the account name twice, and spelled it. I heard him typing, slow, two fingers by the sound of it.

"There's no Drummond," he said. "Not as a rider, not as a driver. No account under that name, no trips to or from Alder Close with that profile. I've pulled your history for the last fourteen days. Every fare you've taken is matched to a named passenger with a payment on file."

"Then look at Harcastle Road," I said. "The underpass. The car park behind the infirmary."

More typing. Somewhere behind him a door closed, and the sound of it went on a little too long, as if the room were larger than a room ought to be.

"What I have," said Vernon, "is you. You've been logged in for six hours, Mr Whitlow. Same stretch of Harcastle Road. Your location hasn't moved since eleven last night, and your status has not changed. It still shows you available." He paused. "Are you at the car now?"

"I'm in my garden."

"Yes," he said. "That's what's odd about it."

I waited for him to suggest a doctor, or a rest. He did neither. The typing had stopped, and the line carried only the thin sound of an open connection, the sound of a long corridor. I counted nine seconds. I was going to say his name when he spoke again, and his voice had lost its flatness. It had become careful.

"I'm going to tell you something that is not in the script. I looked at the wrong screen. The account exists. It was never deleted, only flagged, and I am looking at the flag now." A breath. "Harold Drummond. He drove a cab on Harcastle Road for twenty-two years, and in November 1987 he went out on a wet night and was not seen again. The cab was never found. The account was opened for him afterwards, Mr Whitlow. Opened. Nobody here can tell me by whom."

"That is not possible," I said, and heard how little it was worth.

"There's a note on the flag. Head office has been told that the application fails in one circumstance only. When a ride is marked completed that was never started." The corridor sound swelled behind him. "Mr Whitlow, did your app congratulate you last night?"

I did not answer. Down by the fence the bean poles ticked in the wind, and in the coat on the hook the work phone, which I had not touched, gave a single soft chime.

• • •

I did not answer the supervisor. I let the line run on, the corridor sound and Vernon Hargreaves breathing in it. I took the work phone out of the coat on the hook and read what it said. *Trip completed. Thank you for driving, Douglas. You earned £0.00.* There was a rating beneath it, five stars, and no name against it.

"Mr Whitlow?"

"I'm here."

"Then I'll say the rest of it. The logs show your app has dropped out eleven times in three nights. Each time, directly afterwards, the trip is marked complete. Nobody has ever started one." He cleared his throat. "I would not take another request."

I thanked him. I ended the call. I stood among the bean poles with the rain beginning again, and I laid the three nights out in a row, as I would have laid out a week's takings.

He had never wanted to go anywhere. That was the thing I had missed. He had given me an address that was not in the system, and an address that does not exist cannot be reached, and so the journey could never end. That was why he had never once asked me to hurry. He had asked me only to be easy with the silence.

He had moved from the back seat to the headrest, and from the headrest to my shoulder, one reach of the arm at a time. Each reach had been made in the four or five seconds when the display froze and the road stopped being a road. I had taken those seconds for faults. They were the only seconds in which the car belonged to nobody, and he had been using them as a man uses a gap in a hedge.

He was not a passenger. He was a driver who had lost his seat in 1987, on a wet night, on that same stretch of tarmac, and he was working his way back to the wheel.

I ought to have deleted the application. I ought to have sold the car. I did neither, and I have thought since about why, and the honest answer is that I wanted to be certain. A man will walk into a good deal for the sake of certainty.

At ten past eleven that night, with the work phone clipped back into its mount on the dash, it chimed again. *New request. Harcastle Road underpass. 4 min.* The account name was blank.

I drove there with the wipers on their slowest setting. The underpass is two hundred yards of brick and sodium light, with a drain at the lowest point that has been overflowing since the council last mentioned it. I stopped at the mouth, set the handbrake, and looked down into it. The signal bar on the screen had already shrunk to a single stroke. I watched it flicker. The back seat was empty, and the mirror showed me only my own face.

I turned the heater off. I did not want warmth to confuse what came. Then I pressed the button on the side of the handset and held it until it asked whether I was sure, and I said aloud, "Yes," as if someone had asked me.

The screen went black. The little blue light on the mount, which had been lit for three years, went out.

I released the handbrake, put the car into gear and rolled forward into the underpass. Behind me, with no sound of a door, the rear seat took a man's weight and settled.

• • •

The hand on mine was cold in a way I can only call dry. There was no damp in it, though the whole city outside was running with rain. It lay over my knuckles on the gear stick and the weight of it was exact, each finger placed, as a man might rest his hand on a thing he had owned for many years.

I had thought I would speak. I had prepared a sentence in the car park at home, something about what he wanted, and whether he could say it plainly now that there was no signal to interrupt us. I did not say it. The engine idled. The dashboard, which I had not touched, lost its brightness by degrees. First went the clock, then the fuel gauge, then the small orange lamp for the oil. After that the only light came from the sodium lamps at the mouth of the underpass, and then not even that, for the car had rolled further in than I had meant it to.

The seat behind me creaked as it gave up its weight, and the seat beside me creaked as it took it, though I had heard no one pass between. I did not look. I looked at the windscreen, at the brick curving overhead, at the water running down to the drain. I could smell old upholstery and the sweetish stale smell of a cab that has been smoked in for decades. My own car had never smelled of either.

"Mind the quiet," said a voice beside me, mild and dry. "Most don't."

The hand lifted from mine. I heard the click of a seat belt, mine, being undone, and I felt myself rise, or be raised, with no more effort than a coat being taken from a peg. There was a draught of cold air, a door that did not open, and the sound of the gear lever being worked by someone who knew exactly how stiff it was.

Then the screen in its mount, dead a moment before, lit by itself.

The light was white and very bright after the dark. I had to blink before I could read it. I was sitting upright in the back seat, behind the passenger side, where the vinyl was cracked in a long diagonal. Across my chest ran the belt, drawn snug and clicked home by hands that were not mine. I tried my arms. They moved. I did not try the door.

In the driver's seat sat a grey head, bare and narrow, the hair combed flat with something that had dried long ago. Two hands rested on the wheel at ten and two. The wipers began, slowly, on their own. Beyond the glass the underpass was no longer an underpass but a road I did not know, lit and empty, and the rain fell on it without a sound.

The mirror showed me nothing at all. Only the screen spoke, in its small clean letters:

*Trip started. Pickup: 14 Alder Close.*

It was my address. The indicator ticked, left, left, and Harold Drummond drove me home.

item.title: The Larkspur Cylinders
item.description: A bell-ringer takes a garret in a fog-bound lodging house and finds a phonograph cylinder bearing his own voice, begging forgiveness for a drowning he never committed. Each night brings another recording, and every prophecy on them comes true.
item.content:encoded:
The cylinder had been left behind by the man who kept the garret before me. He had gone in the night, owing a fortnight, and had taken his boots and his hat and nothing else. Mr. Wetherby let the room to me on the Tuesday, and on the Wednesday I found the cylinder in the drawer of the washstand, wrapped in a flannel that smelled of camphor and tallow. The label was brown with age. It read, in a thin clerkly hand, *Larkspur, No. 1*.

The phonograph stood on the sill, under the window, its brass horn turned to the room. It had come with the garret, like the damp patch over the bed and the sixth stair that cried out when trodden. I had never wound it. I had my bell to wind, and my father's ledger to puzzle over, and on that night I wanted only to sit and not think of the quarter-day.

The fog had been in the Larkspur since four o'clock. It stood against the glass and gave the lamp a yellow ring, and below me the foghorns on the river called to one another, one low, one lower. I slid the cylinder onto the mandrel. I turned the crank eleven times, because I count what I turn. I lowered the stylus.

First came hissing, and then a breath, taken close.

"Forgive me," said a voice. "Please. I have carried it so long."

It was my voice. I do not say it resembled mine. I know my own voice as I know the weight of the rope in my hands: the flat northern vowels, the catch before a hard consonant. I put my fingers to my throat and felt nothing move there. The speaker went on, tender and low, as a man speaks to a sick child.

"I never meant the water to take him. I held his sleeve as long as I could. You must believe that I held it. Say that you forgive me for the drowning, and I will ask for nothing more."

I stood up. The chair went over behind me. I did not set it right.

There was a silence on the cylinder, and in it the sound of a clock, a slow clock with a loose pendulum, such as hangs in the parlour downstairs. Then a second speaker answered, calm, unhurried, and dry as paper.

"I forgive you, Desmond. Of course I do. Sit down now. It is finished."

It was Mr. Reginald Wetherby. I had heard him on the stairs not two hours before, saying that the gas was not to be wasted. He had said nothing to me of water, or of a sleeve, or of forgiveness. I have never drowned any man. I have never stood on a quay at night and watched a hand go under. I have rung the bell of St. Anselm's every Sunday of my life, and the only thing I have ever dropped into the Mire is a hymn-book.

The stylus ran off the end and clicked, and clicked, and clicked.

I did not lift it. I sat down upon the bed with my hands between my knees and listened to the clicking. The lamp began to gutter. The yellow ring shrank on the glass. And the horn, though it was silent, went on saying *sit down now*.

• • •

I found Mr. Wetherby in the passage by the parlour door the next morning, trimming the wick of the hall lamp with a pair of small silver scissors. I had not slept. I had carried the cylinder down in my coat pocket and I held it out to him in my palm, as one holds out a coin to a beggar one does not trust.

"Someone has been at my machine," I said. "There is a voice on this. It is mine. It speaks of a drowning."

He did not look at the cylinder. He looked at my face, and then he smiled, slowly, with the lips only, and set the scissors down upon the shelf beside the barometer.

"You are pale, Mr. Marchbanks. The fog gets into the sleeping-rooms. I have always said so." He took out his watch and opened it. "The quarter-day is the twenty-fifth. Your father's sum stands at forty-one pounds, six shillings, and I am a patient man, but I am not a charitable one. Good morning."

He went into the parlour. The clock with the loose pendulum began its slow knocking behind the door, and I stood in the passage with the cylinder in my hand until the lamp, which he had trimmed, burned smokeless and steady.

The next night there was another on the sill. It lay in the dust beside the window-catch, brown and fine-ribbed, and the window was latched from within. I told myself I would not play it. I played it before the church clock struck eleven.

It was my voice again, and quieter. It said that the sexton, old Pettigrew, would cough three times during the Tuesday matins, and that the third cough would break the Creed. It said that Mr. Wetherby would stop me on the stairs at noon and name forty-three pounds, not forty-one, for the interest. Then it said, *I did not mean him to go under, Reginald. I took hold of his sleeve. It was wet wool, and it came away in my hand.*

On Tuesday Pettigrew coughed three times, and the third broke the Creed. At noon, on the stairs, a hand touched my elbow, and a dry voice said, "Forty-three pounds, Mr. Marchbanks." I did not answer. I went up and found the fourth cylinder waiting.

So it went for seven days. Each night a brown cylinder; each day its prophecy, kept as faithfully as a tide-table. The cooper's dog; the broken rung of the belfry ladder; the very word Wetherby used for my lateness, which was *negligent*. And between the prophecies the drowning grew.
